title: War & Peace
hook: War is politics at its most extreme — organized violence between groups. Understanding why it happens, and how peace is kept, is central to the study of states.
key_points: War is large-scale organized armed conflict, usually between states or organized groups.
Theorist Clausewitz called it 'the continuation of politics by other means.'
Causes range from security fears and resources to ideology, territory, and miscalculation.
Peace is more than the absence of war — it can rest on deterrence, cooperation, or shared institutions.
content_html: War is politics carried to its most violent extreme: large-scale, organized armed conflict, classically between states but also between a state and organized groups within or across borders. The 19th-century theorist Carl von Clausewitz captured its political nature in a famous phrase — war is "the continuation of politics by other means" — making the point that war is not the breakdown of policy into senseless violence but the pursuit of political aims through force when other means have failed. Studying war is therefore inseparable from studying states, power, and their interests.
extra_html: Why wars happen has occupied thinkers for as long as there have been wars, and Encyclopaedia Britannica surveys the range of explanations. Some emphasize security and fear — in an anarchic world with no authority above states, each must provide for its own defense, and the steps one takes to feel safe can frighten others into arming, a spiral sometimes called the security dilemma. Others point to competition over resources and territory, to ideology and nationalism, to domestic politics, or simply to miscalculation, where leaders stumble into wars neither side wanted. Just as important is the flip side: peace. Peace is not merely the temporary absence of fighting but something that has to be actively maintained — through the balance of power and deterrence that make war too costly, through diplomacy and cooperation that resolve disputes short of violence, and through shared institutions and economic ties that give states reasons to keep the peace. Much of international politics is, in the end, the ongoing effort to manage conflict and sustain that fragile peace.

related.title: Diplomacy & War
related.hook: States pursue their interests on a spectrum that runs from the conference table to the battlefield. Diplomacy and war are two ends of the same toolkit.

related.title: Sovereignty Among Nations
related.hook: Inside its borders a state is supreme — but in the world of states there's no higher ruler. That gap, called anarchy, shapes everything about international politics.

related.title: Nuclear Weapons & Deterrence
related.hook: How do you stop a war you could never survive? The nuclear age answered with a chilling paradox: build weapons so terrible that no one dares use them.

related.title: Why Ceasefires Break Down
related.hook: A ceasefire stops the shooting. It does not make peace. The difference — and the danger — lies in everything a quick deal leaves out.

flashcards.prompt: How did Clausewitz famously describe war?
flashcards.back_html: As "the continuation of politics by other means" — war pursues political aims through organized force rather than negotiation.

flashcards.prompt: Which of these is offered as a cause of war?

choices.text: Security fears, resources, ideology, territory, or miscalculation

flashcards.explanation_html: Wars arise from many interacting causes, from fear and resources to ideology, territorial disputes, and simple misjudgment.

flashcards.prompt: Why is peace described as more than just the absence of war?

choices.text: Lasting peace rests on deterrence, cooperation, or shared institutions
Because peace and war are identical
Because peace requires no effort at all

flashcards.explanation_html: A durable peace is actively maintained through balances of power, cooperation, and institutions — not merely a pause in fighting.
